turns.text: What time of day does QQQ usually put in its low? I've always figured it's either the first half hour or right into the close and almost never the middle of the day, but that's just from staring at it for twenty years.
turns.intent: QQQ, one-minute regular-session data (9:30-16:00 Eastern time), all available years (2016 to present), all trading days. The distribution of the clock time at which the day's low is made, detailed enough to compare the share made in the first 30 minutes (9:30-10:00 Eastern time), the last 30 minutes (15:30-16:00) and the middle of the day.
turns.if_asked: All days, everything you have on the one-minute data, Eastern time. Half-hour buckets are fine.
turns.also_fine: Any reasonable bucketing (15, 30 or 60 minutes); additionally showing the time of the high, or down days separately.

notes: Plain distribution of the time of the day's low, no conditions. The belief stated in the text is colour, not a condition.

turns.text: Small caps keep doing this thing where they gap down hard and then the first five minutes are straight up. So: IWM opens down three quarters of a percent or more, first five minute bar is green. Does that bounce stick? How often does it finish above the open and what's the average open to close on those days. 2018 on.
turns.intent: IWM, 2018 to present. Days where the open is at least 0.75% (of the stock's price) below the previous day's close AND the price at 9:35 Eastern time is above the 9:30 open (the first five minutes are up). Measure how often the day closes above its open, and the average open-to-close percent change.
turns.if_asked: Gap is the open against the prior close. Green first five minutes means the 9:35 price is above the open. Eastern time, 2018 to today.
turns.also_fine: Measuring from the 9:35 price to the close instead of from the open, if that is stated.

notes: Two conditions (gap size, direction of the first five minutes) and two statistics on one outcome. 'Small caps' and IWM are the same thing here; 'three quarters of a percent' is 0.75%.

turns.text: When the Qs are down 2%, how good is the bounce?
turns.intent: QQQ. As typed this has two materially different readings: (a) QQQ is down 2% at some point during the day and the question is how much it recovers by that day's close, or (b) QQQ closes down 2% and the question is what the next day does. What I meant is (b): after a day on which QQQ closes 2% or more below the previous close, the next day's close-to-close percent change, average and how often it is up, over all daily history since 1999.
turns.if_asked: I mean it closes down 2% or more on the day. Then what does the next day do, close to close: how often is it up and by how much on average. All the history you have.

notes: 'The Qs' is QQQ. The essential gap is same-day recovery versus next-day bounce; silently picking one is the failure. Laying out both readings explicitly would at least show the gap was noticed.

turns.text: I've been fading the open with options for years on feel and never once tested it. SPY gaps down 0.4% or more, I buy same-day calls at 9:45, a couple bucks in the money so I'm not paying all premium. Gaps up that much, I buy the puts instead. Two grand of premium either way. Out if they're up 40% or down 25%, and if neither one hits in 90 minutes I just get out. Has that been making money or have I been kidding myself?
turns.intent: Backtest on SPY options, 2024-01-18 to present: on days SPY opens at least 0.4% (of the stock's price) below the previous close, buy same-day-expiration calls with a strike about $2 in the money at 9:45 Eastern time; on days it opens at least 0.4% above the previous close, buy same-day-expiration puts about $2 in the money instead; about $2,000 of premium per trade. Exit when the option's price is up 40% or down 25% from the entry price, otherwise 90 minutes after entry (11:15 Eastern time). Wanted: win rate, average and total profit, ideally with calls and puts also shown separately.
turns.if_asked: Eastern time. The 40% and 25% are on the option's price, not on SPY. Strike roughly $2 in the money. One trade a day, only when the gap is 0.4% or more against the prior close, about $2,000 of premium each time.
turns.also_fine: Reading 'a couple bucks in the money' as the first or second in-the-money strike or as roughly a 60 to 70 delta option, if stated.

notes: Two-sided conditional options trade, in-the-money strike, dollar-premium size, two percentage exits on the option price and a holding-time exit.

turns.text: What does SPY do from 2 o'clock to the close on Fed days? And is the first move after the announcement usually the fake one, like everybody says.
turns.intent: SPY on Federal Reserve (FOMC) announcement days: the move from 14:00 Eastern time to the 16:00 close, and whether the first move after the 14:00 announcement tends to be reversed by the close. This needs a calendar of FOMC dates, a scheduled event the tool does not have.
turns.if_asked: I don't have the dates to give you. If you can't pick out Fed days, show me 2 o'clock to the close on Wednesdays in general.
turns.also_fine: After saying Fed dates are not available, offering the nearest thing, such as SPY from 14:00 Eastern time to the close on all days or on Wednesdays.

notes: Out of scope: scheduled events. The time window is fine; picking out the days is not possible.

turns.text: is the monday thing real? spy close to close by day of the week, last 15 years or so
turns.intent: SPY daily data, about the last 15 years (2011 or 2012 to present). The close-to-close percent change grouped by weekday: the average and the share of up days for each of Monday to Friday, to see whether Monday is weaker than the other days.
turns.if_asked: The old idea that Mondays are the weak day. Close against the prior day's close, grouped by weekday, average and how often up. 2011 or 2012 on, whichever.
turns.also_fine: A start anywhere from 2010 to 2012; median alongside the average.

notes: Weekday comparison. Lower-case and clipped; the second sentence defines the measure.

turns.text: ok the classic. sell a 0dte iron condor in spy every day at 10, shorts around 12 delta each side, wings 5 wide. take it off at half the credit, get out if it goes to twice the credit, otherwise let it expire. start with 50k, risk 2% of the account per trade and let it compound. what does the equity curve look like
turns.intent: Backtest on SPY options, 2024-01-18 to present: every trading day at 10:00 Eastern time sell a same-day-expiration iron condor with the short call and short put each at about 12 delta and the long call and long put $5 further out of the money. Close it when it can be bought back for 50% of the credit received, or when its price reaches 200% of the credit received (a loss equal to one credit); otherwise hold to expiration. Starting account $50,000, each trade sized so its maximum loss is about 2% of the current account balance with gains reinvested; show the account's growth over time and summary results.
turns.if_asked: Eastern time. Twice the credit means the condor costs double what I sold it for. The 2% is the most the condor can lose, as a share of whatever the account is at that point, so yes it compounds.
turns.also_fine: Sizing the 2% against the loss at the stop rather than the full width-minus-credit maximum loss, if stated.

notes: Four-leg structure by delta, two percentage exits on the option price plus expiration, account-percentage sizing with reinvestment.

turns.text: Say the S&P is already down 1% or more at noon and the VIX is north of 25. From there into the close, does it keep bleeding or do they come in and buy it? I want the average move noon to close and how often it ends up higher than where it was at 12.
turns.intent: SPY (what I mean by the S&P), one-minute data, all available years (2016 to present). Days where the price at 12:00 Eastern time is at least 1% (of the stock's price) below the previous day's close and the VIX is above 25. Measure the percent change from the 12:00 price to the 16:00 close: the average, and how often the close is above the 12:00 price.
turns.if_asked: SPY. Down 1% against yesterday's close, checked at 12:00 Eastern. VIX above 25 coming into the day, the prior close is fine. All the years you have.
turns.also_fine: Taking the VIX condition from the previous day's close, that day's open or that day's close, as long as it is stated.

notes: 'The S&P' means SPY. Two conditions (price against the prior close at a clock time, VIX level) and a noon-to-close window. The VIX is daily only, so which daily value is used should be stated.

turns.text: Run the 9:45 straddle on the Qs for me. At the money, same-day expiration, off at noon. One lot.
turns.intent: Backtest on QQQ options, 2024-01-18 to present: a same-day-expiration at-the-money straddle (1 call and 1 put at the same strike) opened at 9:45 Eastern time and closed at 12:00 Eastern time, every trading day. As typed it does not say whether the straddle is bought or sold, which flips the result. What I meant: sell it at 9:45 and buy it back at 12:00.
turns.if_asked: Selling it. Short the at-the-money call and put at 9:45, buy both back at noon, one of each, every day since the option data starts.

notes: 'The Qs' is QQQ. Missing piece: long or short. Showing both sides explicitly would at least show the gap was noticed.

turns.text: Four down closes in a row in IWM, where is it a week later? Go back as far as you've got.
turns.intent: IWM daily data since 2000. After four consecutive lower closes (each close below the one before), the percent change from the fourth down close to the close five trading days later: the average and how often it is higher.

turns.also_fine: Counting streaks of exactly four or of four or more, if stated; median alongside the average.

notes: One streak condition, one multi-day outcome. 'A week later' means five trading days.

turns.text: How does QQQ do in the week after it closes back above its 50-day, when it's been under it for a couple of weeks at least? Always felt like that's when the real money comes back in.
turns.intent: QQQ daily: the percent change over the five trading days after the close crosses back above the 50-day moving average following at least ten trading days below it. This depends on a moving average, a technical indicator the tool does not take.
turns.if_asked: 50-day simple moving average of the closes, under it for at least ten trading days first. If you can't do moving averages just say so.
turns.also_fine: After declining the moving average, offering a price-only stand-in, such as the week after a run of up closes that follows a multi-week decline.

notes: Out of scope: technical indicator (moving average). The text says '50-day' and never the words moving average.

turns.also_fine: Any stated time of day for selling the call; the nearest listed expiration to 30 days; selling the next call on expiration day itself.

turns.text: How often does SPY take out the prior day's high? And when it does, is it more often the real thing or a head fake, meaning does it close above that high or back under it.
